title: Thomas Mann's other fatherland
gist: Prompted by Pawlikowski's film Fatherland, a classicist traces Thomas Mann's ambivalent relationship with Poland and the East: hostility to the liberal West, fascination with and colonial-style superiority toward the Slavic world, and political opportunism. Cultural history with no direct market content.

insights.claim: Mann's 1927 Warsaw visit at the invitation of Polish PEN treated him as a semi-official envoy of the Weimar Republic, which refused to accept its Polish border, called Poland a Saisonstaat, conspired with Soviet Russia at Rapallo (1922) and waged a trade war on Poland from 1925 to 1934.
insights.speaker: Mateusz Stróżyński
insights.so_what: Historical background on the persistent German-Polish tension in Central Europe.
insights.locator: The political context of the visit is worthy of note

insights.claim: Mann's private 1918-21 diaries show an incoherent mix of views: hatred of the liberal, rationalist West (the Entente), fantasies of a German-Soviet alliance, antisemitic remarks, approval of military dictatorship over mob rule, and a 1918 note that Germans would 'correct the injustice' of lost territories by peace or war.
insights.speaker: Mateusz Stróżyński
insights.so_what: Illustrates how resentment over Versailles fed German revisionism, even in a later liberal icon.
insights.locator: In the diaries we find, quite apart from Mann's astonishing levels of narcissism

insights.claim: Mann wrote flattering letters to the Soviet Literary Society in 1937, praising the Soviet constitution, though he knew its author Bukharin had been arrested, because he craved esteem and avoided making enemies among writers.
insights.speaker: Mateusz Stróżyński
insights.so_what: Shows how prestige-seeking intellectuals can legitimise regimes they privately distrust.

themes.theme: West-East imagery and German colonial superiority

insights.claim: Bismarck's Prussian Settlement Commission, created in 1886, aimed to settle Germans in Polish territories and eradicate Polish culture, and its Poznan headquarters was built in 1908-10, shortly before Mann's Venice stay that inspired Death in Venice.
insights.speaker: Mateusz Stróżyński
insights.so_what: Background for the depth of Polish historical grievance toward Germany.

insights.claim: The author argues Mann's works treat the East (Madame Chauchat, Pribislav Hippe, Tadzio) with a mix of erotic fascination and a German sense of colonial superiority, with Western Bildung depicted as conquest of the East, as in Frederick II's annexation of Silesia.
insights.speaker: Mateusz Stróżyński
insights.so_what: Cultural lens on German attitudes toward Central and Eastern Europe.

insights.claim: The 'Slavic soul' is a purely Russian construct that has infuriated Central European writers from Conrad to Kundera, yet still retains currency in western Europe.
insights.speaker: Mateusz Stróżyński
insights.so_what: Western Europe still conflates Central Europe with Russia, a bias that shapes policy intuitions.
insights.locator: The 'Slavic soul' is a purely Russian construct

insights.claim: Polish critics Birkenmajer and Iwaszkiewicz objected that Mann's 1927 comparison of Goethe and Schiller to Dostoyevsky and Tolstoy implied Poland should be understood through Russia, whereas Mann's 1926 Conrad preface showed he knew Poland 'chose the West'.
insights.speaker: Mateusz Stróżyński
insights.so_what: Poland's self-identification as Western is long-standing and bears on its foreign-policy orientation.
insights.locator: In one of his speeches delivered for the Polish PEN Club in 1927

insights.claim: Pawlikowski won Best Director at Cannes in May 2026 for the black-and-white Fatherland, about Mann's postwar return to Germany, completing a trilogy with Ida (2013) and Cold War (2018).
insights.speaker: Mateusz Stróżyński
insights.so_what: Cultural event of note; no direct market impact.
insights.locator: In May of this year, the Polish filmmaker Paweł Pawlikowski

insights.claim: The film presents Mann as an impotent modern intellectual, homeless in both a West Germany of fake denazification and Americanised pop culture and an East Germany turned into a Soviet-like tyranny, symbolising a European culture that may be dying or have committed suicide.
insights.speaker: Mateusz Stróżyński
insights.so_what: Reflects a cultural-pessimist reading of postwar Europe resonant with current identity debates.
insights.locator: Pawlikowski's Fatherland shows us this opportunistic face of Mann
